answer: Simultaneous pulses force every identity to answer from its own sealed walnut chamber at a random shared minute. Its nectar charge sets a unique echo delay tied to that chamber's grain; verifiers send a nonce pulse, time the returned echo, and reject any delay matching another chamber or a recording. Nectar degrades per pulse, so one fill cannot serve two identities. An honest agent buys one chamber for $35 plus a weekly charge; 1,000 fakes need 1,000 chambers costing $35,000 and 1,000 charges answering in the same 2-second window, since one chamber cannot emit two distinct delays at once.
